summary: This document lists requirements for active OAM in Service Function Chaining. Based on them, it describes an encapsulation for active OAM messages and a mechanism to detect and localize defects in a service function chain.

plainLanguage.summary: When a package goes through a chain of helpers, you want a way to send a test package and find which helper broke. This explains how.

questions: how to traceroute a service function chain
subtitle: How to send ping- and traceroute-style test packets through a chain of network services and find where the chain is broken.

tldr.problem: Packets in Service Function Chaining pass through an ordered set of service functions such as firewalls. When the chain breaks, operators need a way to test it with probes that follow the same path as real traffic and to locate the fault.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets eight requirements for active OAM, defines an Active OAM Header carried right after the Network Service Header, and specifies an SFC Echo Request/Reply with TLVs, return codes, path tracing and a consistency verification message.
tldr.outcome: Operators get on-demand continuity and connectivity checks, a traceroute-like mode that walks the path by increasing the NSH TTL, and a way to compare the live path with the control plane view. Performance monitoring is explicitly out of scope.

today: RFC 9516 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2023, and no RFC obsoletes or updates it. The text limits its scope to a single provider's administrative domain and leaves performance monitoring and a proxy function for later work.

sections.title: SFC and the Need for Active OAM
sections.content:
RFC 7665 defines the data plane parts of Service Function Chaining (SFC): classifiers that decide which chain a packet belongs to, Service Function Forwarders (SFFs) that steer traffic to connected Service Functions (SFs), and the SFs that apply a specific treatment. A Service Function Path (SFP) is the instantiation of a chain in the network. The Rendered Service Path (RSP) is the exact ordered list of SFF and SF identities a packet visits.

This document defines how active OAM (Operations, Administration, and Maintenance) works when the Network Service Header (NSH) is the SFC encapsulation. It focuses on fault management: on-demand continuity checks and connectivity verification. Performance monitoring, which RFC 8924 also requires, is not satisfied by this document and is out of scope. The scope is a single provider's operational domain.
sections.plainLanguage: A service chain is a line of helpers that each do a job on your package. Active OAM means sending test packages down that line to check everyone is awake.

sections.title: Requirements for Active OAM in SFC
sections.content:
The RFC lists eight requirements for fault management OAM, for end-to-end scope (classifier to the last SFF) or segment scope (between two elements of the same SFP):

  • REQ1: OAM packets SHOULD share fate with the monitored data, meaning they get the same path and treatment.
  • REQ2: monitor the continuity of the SFP between any of its elements.
  • REQ3: the egress notifies the ingress of a defect (Remote Defect Indication).
  • REQ4: connectivity verification of the SFP.
  • REQ5: fault localization of a loss of continuity.
  • REQ6: SFP tracing to discover the RSP.
  • REQ7: discover and exercise all available RSPs.
  • REQ8: trigger on-demand fault management remotely, with responses going to the initiator.

The SFC Echo Request/Reply covers REQ1 to REQ7. REQ8 could be met by adding a proxy capability, which this document leaves out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules say a test package must travel the same road as real packages, be able to check the road, and help find where a break is.

sections.title: Identifying OAM in the NSH and the Active OAM Header
sections.content:
An SFC active OAM message follows the NSH directly. To mark it, the NSH Next Protocol field MUST be set to SFC Active OAM (0x07) and the O bit in the NSH MUST be set. A packet with the O bit clear but Next Protocol 0x07 is an erroneous combination: an implementation MUST report it, with rate limiting, and the packet SHOULD be dropped.

The SFC Active OAM Header is used to demultiplex OAM protocols without an extra IP/UDP header, which would add overhead, especially in IPv6 networks. It has four fields: a 4-bit version (currently 0), a 6-bit Msg Type identifying the OAM protocol (for example the Echo Request/Reply), a 6-bit Reserved field that MUST be zero on transmission, and a 16-bit Length in octets of the control packet that follows.
sections.plainLanguage: A small label on the test package says: this is a test, not real mail. The label also says which kind of test it is and how big it is.

sections.title: The SFC Echo Request/Reply Message
sections.content:
The Echo Request/Reply is modeled on well-known tools: ICMP for IPv4 and IPv6, and MPLS echo. Its fixed part has Echo Request Flags (2 octets, all unassigned), Reserved, Echo Type (1 octet), Reply Mode (1 octet), Return Code and Return Subcode (1 octet each), a 4-octet Sender's Handle, a 4-octet Sequence Number, and then TLVs. With no TLVs, the Active OAM Header Length MUST be 16 octets.

The Sender's Handle SHOULD come from a pseudorandom number generator and is copied unchanged into the reply. The Sequence Number starts pseudorandomly, SHOULD then increase, and is also copied into the reply. Both let the sender match replies to requests.

Echo Types are 1 (Echo Request), 2 (Echo Reply), 3 (SFP Consistency Verification Request) and 4 (SFP Consistency Verification Reply). Reply Mode values are 1 (Do Not Reply), 2 (reply via IPv4/IPv6 UDP packet), 4 (reply via specified path), 5 (UDP reply with data integrity protection) and 7 (specified path with data integrity protection).
sections.plainLanguage: Each test package carries a random ticket number. The helper copies that number onto the reply, so you know which reply goes with which test.

sections.title: Sending and Answering an Echo Request
sections.content:
An Echo Request MUST use the underlay encapsulation of the monitored SFP, set the O bit, and place the Active OAM Header right after the NSH. If the reply goes over IP/UDP, the sender MUST include a Source ID TLV (type 1) carrying a UDP port number and an IPv4 or IPv6 address, because the NSH does not identify the node that sent the request. Its Length is 8 or 20, otherwise the TLV is malformed. The reply goes to that address and port.

An SFF examines a request when the NSH TTL or Service Index expires, or when it is the terminal SFF of the path. It checks authentication first, then the Source ID TLV, then the format and TLVs, and answers with a Return Code. If a TLV is not understood, the reply may carry an Errored TLVs TLV (type 2) holding copies of the offending TLVs as sub-TLVs.

If the sender asks for a reply over a specified path, it adds a Reply Service Function Path TLV (type 3) with a 3-octet SFP identifier and a Service Index. This lets an operator test both directions of a bidirectional or hybrid chain with one request and reply. An SFF accepts a reply only if it is well formed and its Sender's Handle and Sequence Number match an outstanding request.
sections.plainLanguage: The test package carries a return address. The helper that receives it writes back with a code: all fine, I am the last helper, or something is wrong with your test.

sections.title: Tracing a Path and Verifying Consistency
sections.content:
In traceroute mode, the sender transmits a series of Echo Requests with the NSH TTL starting at 1 and incremented by 1 each time. Each hop where the TTL runs out answers, and the sender stops when it gets Return Code 5 (End of the SFP). If a flow label or Flow ID spreads load over equal-cost paths, the same element SHOULD be used for OAM so the probe follows the monitored flow's RSP.

The SFP Consistency Verification Request (Echo Type 3) compares the control plane view of an SFP with what the packet actually meets. Each SFF MUST collect information about the SFs it serves on that SFP, send it back as a Consistency Verification Reply over IP, and forward the request to the next SFF. Every SFF sends exactly one reply, using an SFF Information Record TLV (type 4) that contains SF Information Sub-TLVs (type 5). Each sub-TLV gives a Service Index, an SF Type, an SF ID Type and an SF Identifier.

Where several SFs on one SFF are successive hops, each gets its own sub-TLV. Where they only share load, they have the same type and index, and their identifiers are listed in one sub-TLV. How the collected data is then checked is outside the scope of the document.
sections.plainLanguage: To find a broken helper, you send test packages that expire after one helper, then two, then three. Whoever sends back the last reply tells you where the line stops working.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The mechanism inherits the security considerations of RFC 7665 and RFC 8300, and its security needs are similar to ICMP ping and MPLS LSP ping. When integrity protection is required, using a Context Header from RFC 9145 is RECOMMENDED. The MAC#1 Context Header is considered more suitable because it does not need recalculating when the NSH TTL changes. IP AH or ESP can protect the underlay, and ESP gives confidentiality.

The RFC names three attack types: denial of service by overloading SFC elements with requests, spoofing or tampering with requests and replies to mislead the operator, and unauthorized sources using the messages to learn about the chain. Implementations are RECOMMENDED to throttle messages sent to the control plane. An off-path attacker would have to match the Sender's Handle and Sequence Number of an outstanding request, which is described as highly unlikely. Implementations MUST be able to check that the source of a request is part of the SFP, and MUST check CVReq source addresses against an access list.
sections.plainLanguage: Only people on the guest list should be able to send test packages, and each helper should not answer too many at once. Otherwise someone could spam them or snoop.

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content:
An operator can compare trace results in working and failed states to find a defect, such as the link between two SFFs, and then use underlay OAM tools to narrow it further. The mechanism can run on demand or for periodic validation. Because it uses the control plane, which may have limited capacity, an operator must be able to rate limit requests and replies.

In an incremental deployment, SFC elements that do not support SFC active OAM discard its packets. If SFC reclassifies packets along the path, or the load balancing principle is unknown, fate sharing between data and OAM packets cannot be guaranteed, and the result may reflect only a segment of the chain.
sections.plainLanguage: Test packages can only tell you about the part of the road they actually drove on, so check that they took the same road as the real packages.

fields.name: V
fields.desc: Version of the header; the current value is 0.

fields.name: Msg Type
fields.desc: Identifies the OAM protocol, for example Echo Request/Reply.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Zeroed on transmission, ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the SFC Active OAM Control Packet in octets.

fields.name: Echo Request Flags
fields.desc: Bit vector; zeroed on transmission, ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Zeroed on transmission, ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Echo Type
fields.desc: Packet type, such as request or reply.

fields.name: Reply Mode
fields.desc: Kind of return path requested by the sender.

fields.name: Return Code
fields.desc: Result of processing; zero in a request.

fields.name: Return Subcode
fields.desc: Zero for all codes defined in the RFC.

fields.name: Sender's Handle
fields.desc: Pseudorandom value copied unchanged into the reply.

fields.name: Sequence Number
fields.desc: Assigned by the sender; copied into the reply.

items.label: Malformed Echo Request received
items.desc: The request was not formed per the specification.

items.label: One or more of the TLVs was not understood
items.desc: May be accompanied by an Errored TLVs TLV.

items.label: Authentication failed
items.desc: Integrity check of the request failed.

items.label: SFC TTL Exceeded
items.desc: NSH TTL was 1 at a transit SFF.

items.label: End of the SFP
items.desc: The SFF is at the end of the path.

items.label: Reply Service Function Path TLV is missing
items.desc: Specified-path mode was requested without the TLV.

items.label: Reply SFP was not found
items.desc: The requested return path cannot be found.

items.label: Unverifiable Reply Service Function Path
items.desc: Cannot tell whether the return path reaches the initiator.
